title: Alcaraz's Smile After 3:34am Defeat: 'I Suffered, But I Enjoyed'
summary:
Most athletes would be devastated after losing a five-set match at 3:34 in the morning. Carlos Alcaraz smiled instead.

Alcaraz, a 23-year-old Spanish tennis star with seven Grand Slam titles, lost to Ben Shelton at the US Open in a grueling four-hour, 28-minute battle. It was the latest finish in the tournament's history. As he walked down the Arthur Ashe tunnel, cameras caught him grinning widely.

The reason? Alcaraz had been sidelined for over five months with a wrist injury that caused daily pain. He missed the French Open and Wimbledon, and wasn't sure he'd play in New York until a week before the tournament. "I suffered, but I enjoyed, and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling," he explained.

The late finish wasn't unique—several matches at Flushing Meadows ended in the early hours. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, and Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am. "I think it's too much," Alcaraz said. "The last match people stayed, but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed. I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm."

Alcaraz is not alone in dealing with injuries. Britain's Jack Draper struggled with an arm injury and ended his season early, while rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. Alcaraz said he will skip some tournaments in the future to stay "mentally and physically healthy."

This week, he's competing for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London. "When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," he said. "We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch."
why_it_matters: Elite sport is a business built on athletes' bodies, and this story raises a structural question for the next generation of players and fans: how far should tournaments push competitors — and spectators — past midnight in pursuit of television money?

background_read: The US Open is the last of tennis's four Grand Slams — the sport's biggest tournaments, alongside the Australian Open, the French Open and Wimbledon. It is played in late summer at Flushing Meadows in New York City, where the main court, Arthur Ashe Stadium, has a retractable roof so play can continue in the rain.

Night sessions are a selling point for television audiences, but they start in the evening, so long matches can run past midnight. Players and commentators have debated for years whether the schedule should change: some argue late finishes harm recovery and health, while organisers point to ticket demand and broadcast money.

Carlos Alcaraz (a Spanish player who became world number one as a teenager) has been one of the sport's biggest stars. His rival Jannik Sinner (Italy's top player) and Britain's Jack Draper belong to a young generation that plays a punishing, physical style of tennis, and all three have struggled with injuries.

The Laver Cup is a three-day team event, named after Australian tennis legend Rod Laver, in which Team Europe plays Team World. It is being held at The O2 (a large indoor arena in London) and uses a team format that is unusual in a sport normally played by individuals.

perspectives.description: Alcaraz's reaction turned a defeat into a story about gratitude and love of the game. After five months of daily wrist pain, simply competing mattered more than the result, and his attitude has been widely praised as a model of sporting perspective.

A match ending at 3:34am is a health and fairness problem: it disrupts sleep, recovery and preparation for the next round, and it leaves stadium staff, ball kids and fans stranded late at night. Critics say the calendar and night sessions are designed around broadcast revenue rather than athletes.

The Grand Slams have grown into two-week television spectacles, and night sessions are a structural feature, not an accident. Tennis is unusual among major sports in letting matches run without a fixed clock, so the length of a contest — and therefore the finish time — is hard to control in advance.

Possible fixes include earlier start times, fewer night matches, or a hard curfew for play. The Laver Cup's short team format shows an alternative model, and as more top players like Alcaraz openly manage their schedules for health, the pressure to reform the late-night calendar is likely to grow.
